headline: Healey's first Budget cuts energy bills, raises the bank surcharge and speeds up defence spending

terms.meaning: An extra tax on bank profits, added on top of normal corporation tax.

levels.headline: Healey's first Budget cuts energy bills, raises the bank surcharge and speeds up defence spending
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey delivered his first Budget on 28 October 2026, using it to cut pressure on household energy bills, raise taxes on banks and bring forward defence spending.
For energy, the government is abolishing gas standing charges, with targeted mitigations, and sending a £100 payment to around 20 million households as part of a £2.6bn package. The 0% VAT rate on household electricity is extended to 30 June 2027. The bank surcharge rises by 3 percentage points to 6% from January and ends after 15 months, helping to pay for the support.
On defence, the £15bn Defence Investment Plan is fully funded, including £4.7bn that had been unfunded. Healey set 2030 as the target for defence spending of 3% of GDP, with the NATO goal of 3.5% still set for 2035. Support for Ukraine rises by over £10bn, including £500m of urgent military funding this winter.
Healey said there would be no tax rises on wages or dividends. The Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts £15bn of fiscal headroom by 2029/30. Gilt yields eased as he spoke, with the 10-year yield around 5.32%, and bank shares rose.
levels.why: It shows how the new government plans to ease living costs while paying for defence and keeping the bond markets calm.

levels.headline: Healey's first Budget cuts energy bills, raises the bank surcharge and speeds up defence spending

The energy measures include scrapping gas standing charges, a £100 payment to about 20 million households within a £2.6bn package, and an extension of zero VAT on household electricity until 30 June 2027. To help pay, the bank surcharge goes up by three percentage points to 6% from January, for 15 months only.
Defence gets a fully funded £15bn investment plan, which includes £4.7bn that was previously unfunded. The government now aims to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, ahead of the 3.5% NATO target for 2035. Ukraine support rises by more than £10bn, with £500m for this winter.
Healey ruled out higher taxes on wages or dividends. Official forecasters see £15bn of headroom against the government's borrowing rules by 2029/30. Bond yields eased and bank shares rose, though commentators said the defence plan lacked detail.

levels.headline: Budget cuts energy bills, taxes banks and boosts defence

On energy, the fixed daily charge that households pay for gas will be removed. Around 20 million homes will also get £100. Electricity bills will carry no VAT, a sales tax, until June 2027. levels.headline: S&P 500 rises 0.36% to 7,568.92 on Election Day as chip stocks rebound
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed higher on Tuesday 3 November, the last completed trading session, rising 0.36% to end at 7,568.92. The gain ended a three-day losing run on Election Day in the United States.
The Nasdaq Composite, which is heavy with technology firms, climbed 0.83% to 25,372.01 as chip and artificial intelligence stocks rebounded after a sharp sell-off in tech earlier in the week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average moved the other way, losing 197.26 points, or 0.38%, to 51,786.72, with Apple shares weighing on it.
Investors were watching the US midterm elections, in which Democrats were projected to win control of Congress. Stock futures later fell as traders weighed what Democratic gains might mean for areas such as the build-out of data centres. One strategist said the market was not yet out of the woods.
The S&P 500 is a broad index of 500 large US companies and is widely used as a measure of the American market.
levels.why: Share prices show how confident investors are about growth, and they affect pensions and savings.

headline: Bank of England expected to raise Bank Rate to 4% on 5 November as inflation hits 3.5%

terms.meaning: The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences what banks charge and pay.

levels.headline: Bank of England expected to raise Bank Rate to 4% on 5 November as inflation hits 3.5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England announces its next interest rate decision on 5 November, and markets are pricing in a near-certain rise in Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4%, with one source putting the chance at 98%. A further rise in December is also seen as likely.
The expectation follows a jump in inflation. The Consumer Prices Index rose to 3.5% in the 12 months to September, up from 3.1% in August and above the 3.4% economists had forecast. The increase was driven mainly by motor fuel prices, linked to the conflict in the Middle East. Services inflation is also picking up, which raises fears of second-round effects such as higher wage demands.
At its September meeting the Monetary Policy Committee voted 6 to 3 to hold Bank Rate at 3.75%, with three members wanting a quarter-point rise. The Bank aims to keep inflation at 2%. The next inflation figures, for October, are due on 18 November, after the decision.
levels.why: Bank Rate affects mortgages, savings and loans, so a rise changes monthly costs for many households.

headline: Burnham heads to UK-EU summit on 20 November as single market and free movement debate grows

terms.meaning: The EU zone where goods, services, money and people move freely under shared rules.
A group of countries that charge the same taxes on goods from outside the group and none between members.
The right of people to live and work in other countries in a group, such as the EU.

levels.headline: Burnham heads to UK-EU summit on 20 November as single market and free movement debate grows
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will attend a UK-EU summit in Brussels on 20 November, where he will meet European Council President Antonio Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
The government wants deals to cut costs and red tape for British farmers and businesses. Items on the table include a trade deal on food and drink, progress on emissions trading, closer links between energy systems, a youth experience scheme and deeper cooperation on immigration. Brussels also wants tuition fees for European students cut to the rate paid by British students.
Burnham has gone further in discussion than recent predecessors, floating a return to the customs union or the single market and saying the UK could go "all the way". He has also called for an "honest discussion" on free movement. Brussels treats free movement, European Court of Justice jurisdiction and alignment with EU rules as non-negotiable parts of single market membership. Labour's 2024 manifesto ruled out all three.
levels.why: Any new deal with the EU could change trade, prices, travel and work opportunities for people in the UK.

levels.headline: Burnham heads to UK-EU summit on 20 November as single market and free movement debate grows
levels.body:
Andy Burnham will travel to Brussels for a UK-EU summit on 20 November, meeting Antonio Costa and Ursula von der Leyen. His immediate priority is a successful summit, followed by a serious dialogue on longer-term options.
On the agenda are a trade deal on food and drink, an emissions trading agreement, links between energy systems, a youth experience scheme and closer cooperation on immigration. The EU is also pressing for lower tuition fees for European students in Britain. Reports in early October suggested it was unclear whether the two sides could finish deals in time.
The longer-term debate is more charged. Burnham has floated rejoining the customs union or single market and has said the UK could go "all the way". Single market membership would mean accepting free movement, the European Court of Justice and dynamic alignment with EU rules, which Labour's 2024 manifesto ruled out.
levels.why: Any new deal with the EU could change trade, prices, travel and work opportunities for people in the UK.

levels.headline: Burnham heads to UK-EU summit on 20 November as single market and free movement debate grows

Bigger questions sit behind the summit. Mr Burnham has talked about getting closer to the EU, even rejoining the single market. That would mean accepting free movement of people and EU rules, which Labour's 2024 election promises ruled out.

headline: UK unemployment at 4.7% as ONS describes a broadly flat labour market

levels.headline: UK unemployment at 4.7% as ONS describes a broadly flat labour market
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics said on 20 October that the UK unemployment rate was 4.7% in the three months to August 2026, down 0.1 percentage points on both the previous quarter and the year. About 1,712,000 people were unemployed.
The ONS described the labour market as broadly flat through 2026. The employment rate for people aged 16 to 64 was 75.3%, a slight rise, and economic inactivity, covering people neither working nor looking for work, fell by 0.2 percentage points on the year to 20.9%.
Not all of the picture was positive: the number of payrolled employees, measured through tax records, fell over the same period. Regional differences remain large. London had the highest unemployment rate at 6.6%, while Northern Ireland had the lowest at 2.1%.
The next labour market figures are due on 17 November, the day before the October inflation release, and both will be watched by the Bank of England.
levels.why: Jobs data helps show how healthy the economy is, and it feeds into interest rate decisions.

levels.headline: Democrats projected to win the House and Senate in US midterms as count continues
levels.body:
Democrats have been projected to win control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the US midterm elections held on 3 November, though counting was still going on early on 4 November and some races were unresolved.
CNBC reported Democratic gains in several states, including Texas, where James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, and New Hampshire, where Chris Pappas won. Democrats were also projected to flip seats in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio and South Carolina. In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton was projected to beat Vivek Ramaswamy in the race for governor. Coverage framed the vote as a rebuke to Donald Trump's second term, with worries over the cost of living, inflation and the war in Iran weighing on voters. Asian stocks and the dollar fell as the results came in.
levels.why: Control of Congress decides what laws the US president can pass, and it affects markets and global politics.

levels.headline: US strikes Iran's Qeshm Island while mediators push for a deal on the Strait of Hormuz
levels.body:
US forces struck Iran's Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz, on 3 November while mediators worked to bring Washington and Tehran towards a settlement. A US official described the action as defensive, saying it responded to Iranian surface-to-air missile fire at American assets. Iranian media reported five explosions on the island.
Diplomacy continued at the same time. Vice President JD Vance said he was optimistic about a negotiated settlement, and Qatar said it still saw hope for an interim deal as mediators exchanged proposals in real time. Qatar and Pakistan are mediating. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said indirect talks were taking place, and that Iran could reopen the Strait within two days. Iran says its conditions must be met first, with nuclear talks to follow.
Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei warned of a "geographically unrestricted response" if the US attacked again. Shipping through the Strait has been heavily disrupted since the war began in late February, and a June interim agreement has repeatedly broken down.
levels.why: The conflict has disrupted shipping and pushed up energy prices, which affects costs around the world.

levels.headline: Brent crude settles at $103.60 after a second daily fall on hopes of a US-Iran deal

The move followed a much bigger drop on Monday 2 November, when Brent lost 7.6% to settle at $104.77 as the US and Iranian presidents signalled they were open to a diplomatic path. Brent was still trading around $103 on 4 November.
Prices have swung sharply on news of talks and strikes. On Tuesday, oil briefly rose after reports of a US strike on Iran's Qeshm Island, before easing again. Brent ended October at its highest level in six months, and the market has sold off before on settlement rumours, only for fighting to resume.

levels.why: Oil prices feed straight into petrol, heating and transport costs, and so into inflation.

headline: Eurozone inflation at 3.8% as ECB holds rates at 2.5% and Lagarde confirms early exit

levels.headline: Eurozone inflation at 3.8% as ECB holds rates at 2.5% and Lagarde confirms early exit
levels.body:
Eurozone annual inflation jumped to 3.8% in September from 3.2% in August, its highest since September 2023, according to Eurostat. Energy prices were 18.8% higher than a year earlier.
On 29 October the European Central Bank held its deposit rate at 2.5% after raising it in September. President Christine Lagarde said the Governing Council had debated a hike but unanimously chose to wait, and money markets priced about a 67% chance of an increase in December. Lagarde also announced she will leave the ECB next February, months before her term ends.
National October figures point higher. Italy's inflation rose to 5.4%, Spain's held at 4.9% and France's rose to 3.4%, while Germany's fell to 2.8%, helped by a fuel tax cut that took effect on 1 October. One forecaster expects the eurozone figure to reach 4%.
Gas costs are a major factor. Dutch TTF wholesale gas was around €73 per megawatt-hour in early October, about 120% higher than a year earlier, and storage was 71.5% full on 2 October.

levels.body:

The confirmation came after a heavy overnight attack on 3 November in which, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, Russia fired 289 drones and 17 ballistic missiles at Ukraine. Ukraine's own drone campaign continues, and Russia's defence ministry reported intercepting 443 Ukrainian drones in a single night in October.
Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg in late October. Mr Putin said he was ready to resume talks aimed at security after a final settlement, rather than a temporary truce. A local ceasefire in Oleshky, in the Kherson region, has been brokered by Melania Trump, and the White House said she would host representatives of both sides. headline: Poland's Constitutional Tribunal crisis deepens as Tusk and Nawrocki clash over judges

levels.headline: Poland's Constitutional Tribunal crisis deepens as Tusk and Nawrocki clash over judges
levels.body:
Poland's long-running dispute over its Constitutional Tribunal escalated at the end of October, pitting Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government against President Karol Nawrocki.
The core issue is that Mr Nawrocki has refused to accept the oaths of four judges elected by the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, in March 2026, citing procedural concerns. The Tribunal, led by president Święczkowski, ruled in case K 3/26 that the president is not obliged to accept every appointment. The government has challenged that ruling, pointing to the disputed status of some judges on the panel.
On 30 October, judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska ordered a one-month suspension of Mr Święczkowski and vice-president Bartłomiej Sochański. Seven judges entered the Tribunal's headquarters accompanied by State Protection Service officers, and scuffles broke out. Mr Tusk vowed "no compromise" on the rule of law, while Mr Nawrocki called it a serious constitutional crisis.
The European Commission said the appointments lie within the Sejm's power. The dispute dates to 2015.
levels.why: A dispute over court independence tests the EU's rule of law standards and Poland's political stability.

levels.headline: Suspected cyberattacks switch supermarket fridges to defrost in nine European countries
levels.body:
Suspected cyberattacks on 2 November switched supermarket fridges and freezers into defrost mode in nine European countries, and the EU warned of a deliberate attempt to disrupt the bloc's food supply chain.
Euronews names Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland and Italy, and says Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Sweden were also affected. In Belgium, Carrefour reported disruption at about 15 of its 700 stores, and Belgian authorities launched an investigation. In Estonia, hackers pushed the temperature of refrigeration units at one supermarket to 50C.
The incident followed an October attack on hundreds of French supermarkets that caused fridges to overheat, spoiled food and sparked fires. Danfoss supplied the software in both France and Belgium and said customers who had not updated their software were affected.
No group has claimed responsibility and no ransom has been demanded, which has puzzled investigators. Earlier reports counted seven countries; the nine-country figure comes from later coverage and the EU's warning.
